topics.label: AI Literacy & Capability
topics.description: Critical capabilities needed to become AI fluent — frameworks, competencies, and workforce readiness.

articles.title: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review | npj Digital Public Health - Nature
articles.snippet: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review | npj Digital Public Health  Nature
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focused on European public health context; findings on digital competency frameworks may have limited applicability to other sectors or regions outside Europe, though core competency principles may be transferable.
takeaways: Identify which digital competencies are most critical for your public health or healthcare workforce by reviewing the framework's competency domains — this can guide targeted upskilling priorities rather than generic AI training.
Use the scoping review's taxonomy of competencies to benchmark your organisation's current capability gaps and design role-specific learning pathways aligned with European standards.
Consider how the framework addresses both technical skills and softer capabilities (e.g., ethical reasoning, data literacy) — both matter for effective AI adoption in health settings.

articles.title: Mind the gap: an evidence gap analysis of digital literacy within public health systems in the European Union using two different frameworks - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Mind the gap: an evidence gap analysis of digital literacy within public health systems in the European Union using two different frameworks  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focuses specifically on public health systems in EU countries, so findings may not generalise to other sectors or non-EU healthcare systems. Relevance to Australian public health context would require adaptation to local institutional structures.
takeaways: Identify which digital literacy competencies are most lacking in your health organisation by comparing against the two frameworks used in this analysis — this can inform targeted training priorities.
Use evidence gaps identified in EU public health systems as a diagnostic checklist: if similar gaps exist in your Australian health setting, you can learn from EU solutions already being piloted.

Recognise that digital literacy in healthcare spans clinical, administrative, and data competencies — a gap analysis should assess all three rather than assuming one training intervention addresses all needs.

articles.title: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education - Nature
articles.snippet: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education  Nature
articles.generalisability: Limited to middle school context; likely focuses on curriculum design rather than implementation outcomes. Generalisability to workplace AI literacy development or adult learning contexts is unclear without seeing the full article.
takeaways: AI literacy for younger audiences should be embedded within broader digital literacy rather than taught in isolation—consider how this principle applies when designing AI upskilling programs for employees with varying baseline digital competencies.

A holistic framework approach suggests multiple competency domains (technical, ethical, critical thinking) need to be integrated; identify which domains are currently missing from your organization's AI literacy initiatives.

articles.title: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health - Frontiers
articles.snippet: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Findings likely apply primarily to higher education institutions in public health, though faculty development approaches may transfer to other academic disciplines. Geographic scope unclear from title and snippet.
takeaways: Structured faculty development programs can shift staff mindsets from AI resistance to readiness — design targeted training that addresses concerns and builds confidence rather than assuming adoption will follow naturally.
Position faculty as key change agents in building organizational AI literacy; investing in educator upskilling creates a multiplier effect across student cohorts and institutional culture.
Tailor AI literacy initiatives to domain context (public health in this case) to make content relevant and address sector-specific anxieties about AI implementation.

articles.title: Data literacy in the labor market: a systematic review | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: Data literacy in the labor market: a systematic review | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: High — systematic review methodology synthesises evidence across multiple studies and geographies, though specific labour market contexts and educational systems may vary by country.
takeaways: Data literacy is now a foundational workplace competency across sectors; organisations should assess current data literacy levels among employees and identify gaps before designing targeted upskilling programs.
Data literacy training is most effective when integrated into role-specific contexts rather than delivered as generic courses — tailor programs to how different teams actually use data in their work.

Employers should distinguish between technical data skills and interpretive data literacy; the latter (understanding what data means, spotting bias, asking good questions) is often more critical for non-specialist roles.

articles.title: Strategies for developing AI competencies in higher education - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Strategies for developing AI competencies in higher education  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — focuses on higher education context; applicability to workplace AI literacy development programs depends on whether institutional strategies translate to organisational settings.
takeaways: Identify which AI competencies (technical, ethical, domain-specific) are most critical for your employee population before designing training, rather than adopting generic higher education curricula.
Consider blended delivery models combining theoretical foundations with hands-on problem-solving, reflecting evidence-based pedagogical approaches from higher education adapted for adult learners.
Map competency development to career pathways so employees understand how AI skills connect to role progression and organisational strategy.

topics.label: AI & Organisational Psychology
topics.description: Impact of AI on wellbeing, engagement, job crafting, trust, and other org psych constructs.

articles.title: The double-edged mechanism of organizational AI adoption on employee creativity - Frontiers
articles.snippet: The double-edged mechanism of organizational AI adoption on employee creativity  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Cannot assess without access to full article — title suggests empirical research but snippet lacks methodological details, sample size, geographic scope, or sector information.
takeaways: AI adoption in organisations may simultaneously enable and constrain employee creativity depending on implementation approach — consider how your AI systems are designed to either augment or replace human creative thinking.

When introducing AI tools, deliberately assess whether they're creating psychological safety for experimentation or generating pressure to conform to AI-suggested solutions, as this affects creative output.
Design AI integration with explicit attention to preserving employee autonomy and discretion in creative work, rather than assuming more AI automation automatically improves outcomes.

articles.title: Work autonomy mediates associations between medical AI readiness and well being in a three wave nurse study - Nature
articles.snippet: Work autonomy mediates associations between medical AI readiness and well being in a three wave nurse study  Nature
articles.generalisability: Moderate — findings based on nurse population over three waves, but geographic scope and sample size not stated in snippet. Results may be most applicable to healthcare settings but generalisability to other sectors unclear.
takeaways: Nurses' sense of control and decision-making autonomy is critical to wellbeing outcomes when implementing AI — focus change management efforts on preserving or expanding autonomy rather than viewing AI as purely efficiency-driven.

AI readiness training alone is insufficient; organisations should assess whether AI implementation is reducing clinician autonomy, as this may undermine the wellbeing benefits of technical preparation.
Monitor employee wellbeing longitudinally during AI rollout in healthcare settings — autonomy levels are a measurable lever you can adjust to mitigate negative psychological effects.

articles.title: Competing strain and resource pathways linking AI-enabled work systems to employee wellbeing - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Competing strain and resource pathways linking AI-enabled work systems to employee wellbeing  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability cannot be assessed from the snippet provided — geographic scope, sample size, sector, and methodology details are not included.
takeaways: AI-enabled work systems create competing pathways to employee wellbeing: some features reduce strain (e.g., automation of routine tasks) while others increase it (e.g., monitoring or role ambiguity) — organisations need to intentionally design systems to maximise resource gains and minimise strain.

Wellbeing outcomes depend on how AI systems are implemented and governed, not just their technical capabilities — consider the psychological contract, autonomy, and support structures alongside tool adoption.

articles.title: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership - Nature
articles.snippet: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership  Nature
articles.generalisability: Findings may be particularly relevant to paternalistic leadership contexts (common in East Asian organisations), but generalisability to Western hierarchical structures and other leadership styles requires clarification. Sample characteristics and geographic scope not evident from title/snippet.
takeaways: Foster psychological ownership of AI tools among employees—when staff feel ownership over AI systems, they're more likely to actively collaborate with and adapt AI to their work contexts rather than resist or passively comply.
Under paternalistic leadership styles, encourage 'AI crafting' (customising or shaping how AI is used in daily tasks) as a mechanism to deepen employee-AI collaboration and engagement.

Create opportunities for employees to personalise or modify their AI workflows—this sense of agency and ownership may be especially motivating in organisations with directive or mentoring leadership cultures.

articles.title: Psychological safety mediates link between AI adoption and worker depression - PsyPost
articles.snippet: Psychological safety mediates link between AI adoption and worker depression  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Generalisability cannot be assessed from the snippet provided; the original study details (sample size, geography, sector, methodology) are not available in this excerpt.
takeaways: Psychological safety is a critical protective factor when introducing AI tools — workers who feel safe to speak up, ask questions, and admit mistakes show lower depression rates during AI adoption.

Simply deploying AI technology without attention to team psychological safety may inadvertently increase mental health risks; managers should prioritise creating safe spaces for questions and concerns about AI before and during rollout.
Monitor psychological safety metrics as a leading indicator of worker wellbeing during AI transitions, rather than waiting for depression or disengagement to emerge.

articles.title: Dual pathways of generative AI use: role ambiguity and self-efficacy in employee-AI collaboration - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Dual pathways of generative AI use: role ambiguity and self-efficacy in employee-AI collaboration  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear from title and snippet alone; depends on sample composition, size, and sectors studied. Frontiers publications vary widely in methodological rigor and geographic scope.
takeaways: Role ambiguity about how to use AI in your job undermines collaboration — clarify AI responsibilities and expected workflows with your team to reduce uncertainty and boost adoption.
Self-efficacy (confidence in your ability to use AI tools) is a key lever for adoption — provide targeted training and early wins so employees build competence and comfort with generative AI.
Address both the emotional/psychological barrier (self-efficacy) and the structural barrier (role clarity) together; fixing one without the other may limit effectiveness of AI upskilling initiatives.

topics.label: Behavioural Change Frameworks
topics.description: Evidence-based frameworks for driving behaviour change — in the context of AI adoption and workforce transformation.

articles.title: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI - Deloitte
articles.snippet: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI  Deloitte
articles.generalisability: Moderate — Deloitte practitioner perspective likely based on client work across multiple sectors and geographies, but specific evidence base and sample details are not provided in the snippet.
takeaways: Shift organisational change strategy from 'AI adoption' framing (tool implementation) to 'AI adaptation' framing (behaviour and capability development) to better embed new ways of working.
Identify and deliberately shape the human behaviours required for AI success before or alongside technology rollout, rather than expecting behaviours to follow naturally from system availability.
Use structured change management approaches that target mindset, capability, and organisational culture alongside technical implementation to sustain AI use.

articles.title: Dual-path mechanism of AI awareness on employee job crafting: insights from the cognitive appraisal of stress and JD-R perspective | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: Dual-path mechanism of AI awareness on employee job crafting: insights from the cognitive appraisal of stress and JD-R perspective | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet — full methodology details unavailable. Findings depend on sample demographics, organisational context, and whether study is cross-sectional or longitudinal. Geographic scope and sector representation not evident from title alone.
takeaways: AI awareness can trigger two distinct pathways in how employees reshape their jobs: one through perceived threat (stress appraisal) and one through opportunity recognition. Understanding which pathway dominates in your workforce helps you design targeted upskilling or reassurance interventions.

Job crafting (proactively redesigning tasks and relationships) appears to mediate the relationship between AI awareness and outcomes — employees who actively reshape their roles may experience better adjustment. Consider creating formal channels or psychological safety structures that explicitly encourage job crafting conversations when AI tools are introduced.

articles.title: How AI Is Reshaping the Future of Work - Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.snippet: How AI Is Reshaping the Future of Work  Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to be a Stanford perspective piece without specified empirical data or sample. Findings may reflect US higher education and business school biases rather than broader workforce dynamics.
takeaways: Identify specific roles and tasks in your organisation where AI is most likely to create disruption, then design targeted upskilling programs for affected teams before change occurs rather than after.
Frame AI adoption as a behaviour change challenge requiring psychological safety — employees need permission to experiment, ask questions, and make mistakes as they learn new AI-augmented workflows.

Engage employees early in discussions about how AI will reshape their work; those who co-design AI implementation are more likely to adopt new tools and adapt their behaviours compared to those who experience change as something done to them.

articles.title: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear from title and snippet alone — no details provided on sample size, geography, or sectors studied. The approach-avoidance framework may apply broadly to AI adoption contexts, but evidence of cross-sector or cross-cultural validity is not evident from available information.
takeaways: Employees' job crafting responses to AI adoption fall into approach (embracing, actively reshaping role) and avoidance (withdrawing, minimising engagement) patterns — recognising which tendency dominates in your team helps you design targeted support to shift avoidance toward approach behaviours.

Understanding whether employees are psychologically approaching or avoiding AI integration allows you to tailor change communication and upskilling programmes to address underlying motivations rather than imposing top-down adoption strategies.

articles.title: Innovative technologies and workplace collaborations in the energy sector based in the United Arab Emirates - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Innovative technologies and workplace collaborations in the energy sector based in the United Arab Emirates  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — findings are specific to the UAE energy sector and may not generalise to other geographic regions, industries, or organisational contexts. The energy sector has distinct characteristics (capital intensity, technical specialisation, regulatory environment) that differ from other sectors.
takeaways: Identify which collaborative practices and technology adoption strategies used in UAE energy organisations could be adapted to your context — consider how sector-specific factors (regulation, skill profiles, resource availability) differ from the UAE model.
Use insights about workplace collaboration patterns in high-tech energy environments to diagnose current gaps in your own teams' technology integration and information-sharing practices.

Examine how the UAE case study demonstrates the relationship between technology implementation and team collaboration — this can inform whether your behaviour change efforts should prioritise tool adoption or relational/social factors first.

articles.title: Challenge or threat? The double-edged sword effect of AI use on innovative teaching behavior among primary and secondary school teachers in China | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: Challenge or threat? The double-edged sword effect of AI use on innovative teaching behavior among primary and secondary school teachers in China | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Limited to Chinese primary and secondary school context. Findings may not generalise to other cultural contexts with different attitudes toward technology adoption, educational systems, or teacher autonomy. Chinese education policy and school structures differ significantly from Western systems.
takeaways: AI tools can paradoxically inhibit innovation in teaching if educators perceive them as threatening rather than challenging — frame AI adoption as a skill-building opportunity rather than a job risk to shift psychological response from threat to challenge appraisal.

Teacher perceptions of AI capability and control are key leverage points; organisations should invest in transparent communication about AI limitations and ensure teachers retain meaningful decision-making authority over pedagogy to sustain innovative behaviour.

Support structures matter: provide training, resources, and psychological safety alongside AI tools to help educators move from defensive reactions to proactive experimentation with new teaching methods.

topics.label: Fascinating Psychology Research
topics.description: Surprising, counterintuitive, and delightful findings from personality and behaviour research — the kind of study you'd share at dinner.

articles.title: When personality meets surprise: individual differences in memory for unexpected events - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When personality meets surprise: individual differences in memory for unexpected events  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Scope not determined from title and snippet alone — likely laboratory-based study with limited sample, generalisability depends on participant demographics and experimental design not evident here.
takeaways: People with different personality traits remember surprising moments differently — some personality types are better at encoding unexpected events into memory.
Your personality might predict whether you'll vividly recall that shocking moment or gloss over it, suggesting surprise alone doesn't create equal memory for everyone.
The counterintuitive finding: personality traits, not just the surprise factor itself, drive how well we retain novel and unexpected experiences.

articles.title: The science of why friendships keep us healthy - American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.snippet: The science of why friendships keep us healthy  American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.generalisability: High — synthesises broad research on friendship and health outcomes across diverse populations, though specific mechanisms may vary by culture and social context.
takeaways: Strong friendships can be as protective for physical health as exercise and better than some medical interventions — a striking reminder that social connection isn't just 'nice to have' but measurably life-extending.
The health benefits of friendship work both ways: good friends improve your immune function and cardiovascular health, which is why loneliness is genuinely risky, not just emotionally painful.
What makes this fascinating is that quality matters far more than quantity — one or two genuine close friendships deliver more health bang for your buck than a large shallow social network.

articles.title: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe - University of Cambridge
articles.snippet: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe  University of Cambridge
articles.generalisability: High — findings suggest cross-cultural patterns in how personality relates to music taste, though specific musical genres and cultural contexts may vary by region.
takeaways: Personality traits predict music preferences consistently across countries, suggesting that what you listen to reveals something universal about how you think and feel — regardless of where you live.
The study reveals a surprisingly strong link between temperament and taste, meaning your Spotify playlist is less shaped by geography or peer pressure than by who you actually are.
It's counterintuitive that something as culturally specific as music taste — shaped by local radio, family influence, and trends — still maps onto personality in recognisable ways worldwide.

articles.title: New psychology research reveals the surprising relationship between cynicism and power - PsyPost
articles.snippet: New psychology research reveals the surprising relationship between cynicism and power  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Unable to assess — snippet provides only headline without detail on study design, sample size, geographic scope, or methodology.
takeaways: Cynicism and power have a counterintuitive relationship that defies the common stereotype of cynical people being powerless or disconnected.
The finding challenges assumptions about how personality traits like cynicism shape social influence and status, suggesting the relationship is more complex than folk psychology suggests.
This research highlights why studying seemingly negative traits through a scientific lens can reveal surprising truths about human nature and social dynamics.

articles.title: Out of the dark – Psychological perspectives on people's fascination with true crime - Perchtold‐Stefan - 2026 - Wiley & Sons
articles.snippet: Out of the dark – Psychological perspectives on people's fascination with true crime - Perchtold‐Stefan - 2026  Wiley & Sons
articles.generalisability: Moderate — synthesises existing psychological research on true crime fascination, but specific applicability depends on the studies reviewed and their geographic representation.
takeaways: True crime captivates audiences through a psychological 'safe danger' mechanism — it lets us explore threat and mystery from a distance, satisfying our curiosity without real risk.
People's obsession with true crime isn't morbid voyeurism; it often reflects deeper drives like sense-making, control-seeking, and understanding human nature through real-world scenarios.
The psychological appeal cuts across demographics, suggesting true crime taps into universal human needs to process fear, understand deviance, and assert moral judgment in a controlled setting.

articles.title: Which Personality Traits Are Most Important to Employers? - Association for Psychological Science – APS
articles.snippet: Which Personality Traits Are Most Important to Employers?  Association for Psychological Science – APS
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to be a commentary piece without specified empirical data, sample size, or geographic scope. Likely reflects general observations rather than rigorous research findings.
takeaways: Employers prioritise personality traits beyond technical skills, suggesting 'soft skills' matter as much as credentials when hiring — a counterintuitive finding given how much job ads focus on qualifications.
Understanding what employers actually value in personality could reshape how people present themselves in interviews and resumes, flipping the conventional wisdom about leading with experience.
The mismatch between what job seekers think employers want and what employers actually prioritise creates an interesting psychology puzzle about workplace perception and communication.

topics.label: Psychological Safety
topics.description: Research on psychological safety and its role in team learning, AI experimentation, and innovation.

articles.title: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2026 - PwC
articles.snippet: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2026  PwC
articles.generalisability: Broad insights across multiple countries and sectors, though PwC's client base may skew towards larger organisations and professional services. Specific country breakdowns would affect applicability to Australian contexts.
takeaways: Use survey data on workforce concerns to identify psychological safety gaps in your organisation — compare your team's fears and hopes against global trends to pinpoint where trust and open communication need strengthening.

When designing psychological safety interventions, reference specific employee hopes and fears from the survey to make the business case to leadership and ensure initiatives address what employees actually care about.

Consider which fears (e.g. job security, skill relevance, workplace culture) are most acute in your workforce, and design targeted psychological safety measures — such as transparent communication about AI adoption or upskilling opportunities — to address them.

articles.title: When inclusive leadership promotes innovation: the role of team psychological safety and leader power distance orientation - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When inclusive leadership promotes innovation: the role of team psychological safety and leader power distance orientation  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on study design and sample composition (unclear from snippet); findings on psychological safety and inclusive leadership likely applicable across sectors, though power distance effects may vary by organisational culture and national context.
takeaways: Inclusive leadership that reduces perceived power distance strengthens team psychological safety, which in turn supports innovation — consider auditing your own leadership communication style for openness to challenge and idea contribution across hierarchy levels.

Leader power distance orientation (formal vs. approachable) moderates the link between inclusive leadership and psychological safety; teams with leaders who minimise status barriers see greater safety and innovation, suggesting targeted leadership coaching on psychological safety practices could yield measurable innovation gains.

articles.title: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear without access to full methods — the title suggests a correlational study linking AI adoption to depression, but sample size, geographic scope, sectors, and study design are not evident from the snippet alone. Findings may not generalise across different AI implementation contexts or organisational cultures.
takeaways: AI adoption can negatively affect employee mental health if it erodes psychological safety; organisations should proactively monitor wellbeing and create space for employees to voice concerns about AI tools before and during rollout.

Ethical leadership is critical during AI transitions — leaders who model transparency, fairness, and concern for employee welfare can buffer against depression and anxiety by maintaining trust and psychological safety as systems change.

Before deploying AI, assess how the technology might threaten psychological safety (e.g., surveillance, job insecurity, unclear decision-making), and design mitigation strategies such as stakeholder input, transparent change communication, and mental health support.

articles.title: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — BCG analysis likely draws on consulting experience and case studies, but specific sample details, industry scope, and geographic focus are unclear from the snippet provided.
takeaways: Create explicit norms where employees feel safe questioning decisions and admitting mistakes without fear of punishment or embarrassment — this helps level participation across hierarchy and experience levels.

Psychological safety particularly benefits underrepresented or newer team members who might otherwise hold back — measure and track participation patterns to ensure your safety interventions are actually reducing speaking-up barriers for all groups.

articles.title: What is psychological safety at work? Here’s how to start creating it - American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.snippet: What is psychological safety at work? Here’s how to start creating it  American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.generalisability: Moderate — draws on established psychological research but presents general principles without specifying geographic context or organisational sector limitations. Applicability may vary by workplace culture and industry.
takeaways: Start by modelling vulnerability as a leader: admitting mistakes, asking for help, and inviting input normalises psychological safety behaviourally rather than through policy alone.

Establish clear norms that separate the person from the problem—create space for dissent on ideas while maintaining respect for individuals, reducing fear of interpersonal consequences for speaking up.

Conduct a baseline assessment of current psychological safety in your team using anonymous surveys or focus groups before implementing changes, so you can target interventions to the specific barriers your workforce faces.

articles.title: Why Innovation Depends on Intellectual Honesty - MIT Sloan Management Review
articles.snippet: Why Innovation Depends on Intellectual Honesty  MIT Sloan Management Review
articles.generalisability: Limited — conceptual piece without empirical data or specific organizational context; insights are theoretical and may not generalise across different cultures or organizational types.
takeaways: Create explicit norms where team members are expected to voice dissenting views and challenge assumptions without fear of social or professional repercussions — this requires leaders to visibly reward honest disagreement.
Establish feedback mechanisms that separate idea evaluation from person evaluation; critique the proposal, not the proposer, to reduce defensive reactions that stifle candid contribution.

Model intellectual honesty yourself by admitting uncertainty, changing your mind when presented with evidence, and thanking people who respectfully challenge your thinking — this signals that honest expression is genuinely safe.
